govdocs-archive_org-KempisImitationOfChr:
Thomas a Kempis, a German-Dutch monk of the fifteenth century, wrote The Imitation of Christ, the devotional book most read after the Bible itself. This copy follows the Christian Classics Ethereal Library edition in a modern translation. Thomas wrote for monks; the whole Christian world adopted the book.

In four books of short chapters he teaches contempt of the world's vanities, the turning inward of the soul, comfort in suffering, and devotion to the sacrament. The counsel is plain and searching: humility first, and Christ's life as the pattern. Few books have formed so many private devotions across so many centuries, in so many tongues.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAOversightHou:
Mary Russell reported for the Washington Post on a vote that changed Congress: the House of Representatives voted to establish a standing intelligence committee. Until the 1970s, the CIA had answered to small, deferential subcommittees that asked little and were told less.

The Church and Pike investigations changed that mood, and the vote created permanent oversight in the House, matching the Senate's new committee. Russell's article is the news of oversight's birth, reported on the day it happened. It is preserved among the archive's clippings on the long fight to make the intelligence agencies answerable to elected legislators.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Double-CrossGia:
A tabloid-style article promotes Double Cross, a book by Chuck Giancana, brother of Chicago mob boss Sam Giancana, written with the younger Sam Giancana. Its headline claim is blunt: the Mob had sex tapes to blackmail President Kennedy. The article ties the alleged scheme to Frank Sinatra.

Pieces of this kind sold the book by selling its most shocking claim first. Readers should note the form: the article is promotion in tabloid dress, not evidence tested in court. It still shows how the Giancana family story was marketed to the public, scandal at the front.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDirectorisRi: A bound report of proceedings of the President's Commission on the Assassination of President Kennedy survives here as copy 12 of 12. The commission sat in Washington, D.C., and its proceedings were printed in numbered copies for official use. The surviving record identifies the document and its copy number but lists no sessions or testimony, so it stands as one numbered copy of the commission's own record.
